vignette: A chemistry control at +2.2 SD is observed on one control material; a second control is at +2.6 SD (both above the mean).
stem: Which Westgard rule is violated and what action is required?
explanation: Two consecutive controls (or two different controls in the same run) exceeding 2 SD on the same side of the mean = 2_2s rule — a rejection rule indicating systematic error.

rationales.A: 1_2s is a warning for a single control beyond 2 SD; here two controls exceed 2 SD.
rationales.B: Correct: 2_2s violated — reject the run and investigate.
rationales.C: R_4s requires a range exceeding 4 SD between controls (one high, one low).
rationales.D: 1_3s requires one control beyond 3 SD; neither control exceeds 3 SD here.

misconception: The '2' in 2_2s means TWO controls, not one control twice — the classic Westgard trap.
examTraps: 2_2s = two controls, same side, beyond 2 SD → reject.

vignette: A patient's potassium result is 7.8 mmol/L but the sample is visibly hemolyzed; the patient is asymptomatic.
stem: What is the most appropriate action?

choices.text: Report the result as is with no comment
Add a hemolysis comment and/or recollect a fresh sample before reporting

explanation: Hemolysis releases intracellular potassium causing pseudohyperkalemia. Best practice: recollect and/or report with an interpretive comment about hemolysis; never silently report or 'correct' the value.

rationales.A: Reporting a spurious critical value without comment risks inappropriate treatment.
rationales.B: Correct: comment and/or recollection is standard practice.
rationales.C: There is no validated universal correction factor for hemolysis.
rationales.D: Cancelling without follow-up leaves the clinical question unanswered.

misconception: Pseudohyperkalemia is the most common spurious electrolyte result in the lab — always check sample quality.
